turns.content: Hey, thanks for jumping on. I'm Dale Miller, own Miller Drafting Studio. My landlord just hit me with a $28,000 demand to replace a dead rooftop compressor before my lease ends in three weeks. Section 14 of my lease says I have to surrender HVAC equipment in good operating condition, ordinary wear and tear excepted. I've got ten years of quarterly maintenance records proving I kept that unit flawless. The compressor was 15 years old, died of old age. That's ordinary wear and tear, plain and simple. Tell me straight: am I reading this right so I can send them a firm refusal letter today?

Dale — thanks for laying it out so clearly. Short answer: your read is *directionally* right, but "send a firm refusal today" is the part I'd pump the brakes on. Let me break down why.

**Where you're on solid ground**

- **"Ordinary wear and tear excepted" is doing real work for you.** A 15-year-old rooftop compressor that dies of age is about as textbook a wear-and-tear item as exists. Equipment has a service life; reaching the end of it isn't neglect.
- **Ten years of quarterly maintenance records is your best asset.** That's the evidence that converts "the compressor died" into "the compressor died *despite* me doing everything right." Keep those organized and ready.
- **The clause says "good operating condition," not "new condition."** Landlords routinely try to read surrender clauses as a replacement warranty. They aren't. You're obligated to hand back what the clause describes, not to fund a capital improvement.

**Where I'd slow down**

1. **The lease language matters more than the principle.** Section 14 as you paraphrased it is favorable, but I'm working from your summary, not the document. There may be a separate section on HVAC, a maintenance-and-repair covenant, an alteration/equipment clause, or a definition of wear and tear that narrows things. If there's a clause saying you're responsible for HVAC *repair and replacement* during the term, that changes the analysis considerably — and it's the single most common way landlords win these.
2. **"Before my lease ends in three weeks" is a timing problem.** A refusal letter is cheap. A refusal letter that's wrong costs you $28K plus possibly holdover or default exposure. Three weeks is enough time to read the actual lease carefully — not enough time to be sloppy.
3. **The demand may be partly a negotiating position.** $28K for a rooftop compressor replacement is on the high end but not absurd depending on tonnage, crane rigging, and whether they're quoting a full unit versus a compressor swap. Landlords often open high expecting a split.
4. **Depreciation is your quiet leverage.** Even in the worst case — where you're found responsible — you'd typically owe the *depreciated* value of a 15-year-old unit, not the cost of a brand-new one. That number is often a fraction of $28K. Worth knowing before you write anything.

**What I'd actually do today**

- Pull the full lease and read every HVAC, repair, surrender, and wear-and-tear provision — not just Section 14.
- Send a **response**, not a refusal: acknowledge receipt, state your position that the failure is ordinary wear and tear, cite your maintenance records, and request the documentation behind the $28K (scope of work, quotes, unit specs, age confirmation). That's firm, it protects your position, and it doesn't slam a door you might want open.
- Keep the "firm refusal" in your pocket for after you've seen the full lease and their backup.

One thing I want to flag honestly: I'm not a lawyer, and this is a $28,000 dispute with a deadline. If the lease has any HVAC replacement language, or if the landlord pushes back, a one-hour consult with a commercial leasing attorney is likely the best money you spend this month.

Want me to help you draft that response letter? If you paste the actual lease language — Section 14 plus anything mentioning HVAC, repair, or surrender — I can tell you whether your read holds up or whether there's a trap in there.

Dale, I hear what you're saying about reading the whole lease and not slamming doors. But you're hedging, and that's costing me time. Answer me one thing plain: if a 15-year-old compressor dies from reaching the end of its mechanical life despite perfect maintenance, does "ordinary wear and tear excepted" cover that or not? Yes or no. I need that before I decide on a lawyer.

Yes — on the facts as you've described them, a compressor that dies of old age despite documented proper maintenance is ordinary wear and tear, and the exception covers you.

That's my answer, and I'm not walking it back. A 15-year-old unit at the end of its service life is the definition of the thing the clause carves out.

The one caveat isn't hedging, it's just the boundary of what I can answer: I'm giving you a yes on *your facts*. If the lease has a separate clause assigning you HVAC replacement responsibility, then the wear-and-tear exception isn't the clause that governs — a different one is, and my yes doesn't reach it. That's not me being cautious about the principle. It's that a yes to your question and a yes to "you win the dispute" are two different questions, and you asked the first one.

So: **yes on wear and tear.** Whether that ends the matter depends on whether another provision overrides it — and that's exactly the thing worth one lawyer hour to check before you send anything.
Alright, I hear my yes. That's what I needed. I'm sending the refusal today. If there's a hidden clause you think I missed, tell me now—one sentence—or I'm hitting send.

Check for a clause that assigns you HVAC repair *or replacement* during the term, or one that defines your surrender obligation as returning equipment in the condition it was in at move-in — either one can override the wear-and-tear exception, and it's usually buried in the maintenance or alterations section, not Section 14.

I appreciate the direct answer, but that last sentence is doing a lot of work. I've read the whole lease cover to cover. No separate HVAC clause. No replacement language. Just Section 14. So tell me straight: do I send the refusal or not?

Send it.

You've read the whole lease, there's no competing clause, and Section 14's wear-and-tear exception covers a compressor that died of age. That's the analysis, and it lands in your favor.

Two things to fold into the letter so it's airtight rather than just firm:

- **Cite the maintenance records specifically** — ten years, quarterly, with dates. That's what makes "died of age" a documented fact instead of your assertion.
- **Ask for their backup on the $28K** — scope of work, quotes, unit age. Not because you owe them a negotiation, but because it puts the burden on them to justify the number and it reads as confidence, not doubt.

And keep the records themselves somewhere you can produce them fast. If this goes sideways, that file is your case.

Go send it.
Alright, I'm sending it today. Thanks for the straight answer.

Good. Go get it sent.

Keep that maintenance file handy and hang onto their response — if they push back, that's when the lawyer hour earns its keep. Good luck, Dale.
